title: VII. Ilusha
paragraphs: The doctor came out of the room again, bundled up in his fur coat and with his cap on his head. His face looked almost angry and disgusted, as though he were afraid of getting dirty. He cast a cursory glance around the passage, looking sternly at Alyosha and Kolya as he did so. Alyosha waved from the doorway to the coachman, and the carriage that had brought the doctor drove up. The captain darted out after the doctor and, bowing apologetically, stopped him to get one last word. The poor fellow looked utterly crushed; there was a scared look in his eyes.

“Your Excellency, your Excellency ... is it possible?” he began, but couldn't go on, and clasped his hands in despair. Still he kept gazing imploringly at the doctor, as though a word from him might yet change the poor boy's fate.
“I can't help it — I am not God!” the doctor answered offhand, though with his customary air of importance.
“Doctor ... your Excellency ... and will it be soon, soon?”
“You must be prepared for anything,” the doctor said in emphatic, cutting tones, and, dropping his eyes, he was about to step out to the carriage.
“Your Excellency, for Christ's sake!” the terror-stricken captain stopped him again. “Your Excellency, can nothing, absolutely nothing save him now?”

“It's no longer in my hands,” the doctor said impatiently, “but h'mm ...” he stopped suddenly. “If you could, for instance ... send ... your patient ... at once, without delay” (the words “at once, without delay” the doctor uttered with an almost wrathful sternness that made the captain start) “to Syracuse, the change to the new, be-ne-fi-cial climatic conditions might possibly —”
“To Syracuse!” the captain cried, unable to grasp what had been said.
“Syracuse is in Sicily,” Kolya jerked out suddenly by way of explanation. The doctor looked at him.
“Sicily! Your Excellency,” faltered the captain, “but you've seen” — he spread out his hands, taking in his surroundings — “mamma, and my family?”

“N-no, Sicily is not the place for the family — the family should go to the Caucasus in the early spring ... your daughter to the Caucasus, and your wife ... after a course of the waters in the Caucasus for her rheumatism ... must be sent straight to Paris, to the mental specialist Lepelletier; I could give you a note to him, and then ... there might be a change —”
“Doctor, doctor! But you see!” The captain flung his hands wide again in despair, gesturing at the bare wooden walls of the passage.
“Well, that's not my business,” the doctor grinned. “I've only told you the answer of medical science to your question about possible treatment. As for the rest, to my regret —”

“Don't be afraid, apothecary — my dog won't bite you,” Kolya rapped out loudly, noticing the doctor's rather uneasy glance at Perezvon, who was standing in the doorway. There was a note of wrath in Kolya's voice. He used the word “apothecary” instead of “doctor” on purpose — and, as he explained later, used it “to insult him.”
“What's that?” The doctor flung up his head, staring with surprise at Kolya. “Who's this?” He turned to Alyosha, as if asking him to explain.
“It's Perezvon's master — don't worry about me,” Kolya said incisively, again.
“Perezvon?”[7] the doctor repeated, perplexed.
“He hears the bell, but where it is he cannot tell. Good-bye, we'll meet again in Syracuse.”
“Who is this? Who is this?” The doctor flew into a terrible rage.

“He's a schoolboy, doctor, he's a mischievous boy — take no notice of him,” Alyosha said quickly, frowning. “Kolya, hold your tongue!” he cried to Krassotkin. “Take no notice of him, doctor,” he repeated, rather impatiently.
“He needs a thrashing, a good thrashing!” The doctor stamped his foot in a perfect fury.
“And you know, apothecary, my Perezvon might bite!” said Kolya, turning pale, his voice quivering and his eyes flashing. “_Ici_, Perezvon!”
“Kolya, if you say another word I'll have nothing more to do with you,” Alyosha cried peremptorily.
“There's only one man in the world who can give an order to Nikolay Krassotkin — this is the man,” Kolya said, pointing at Alyosha. “I obey him. Good-bye!”

He stepped forward, opened the door, and went quickly into the inner room. Perezvon flew in after him. The doctor stood still for five seconds in amazement, looking at Alyosha; then, with a curse, he went out quickly to the carriage, muttering aloud, “This is ... this is ... I don't know what this is!” The captain darted ahead to help him into the carriage. Alyosha followed Kolya into the room. He was already by Ilusha's bedside. The sick boy was holding his hand and calling for his father. A minute later the captain came back too.

“Father, father, come ... we ...” Ilusha faltered in violent excitement, but apparently unable to go on, he flung his wasted arms around his father and Kolya, uniting them in one embrace and hugging them as tightly as he could. The captain suddenly began to shake with silent sobs, and Kolya's lips and chin twitched.
“Father, father! How sorry I am for you!” Ilusha moaned bitterly.
“Ilusha ... darling ... the doctor said ... you'll be all right ... we'll be happy ... the doctor ...” the captain began.
“Ah, father! I know what the new doctor said to you about me. I saw!” Ilusha cried, and hugged them both again with all his strength, hiding his face on his father's shoulder.
“Father, don't cry. And when I die, take another good boy, another one ... choose one of them all, a good one, call him Ilusha and love him instead of me ...”
“Hush, old man, you'll get well,” Krassotkin cried suddenly, in a voice that sounded angry.

“But don't ever forget me, father,” Ilusha went on. “Come to my grave ... and, father, bury me by our big stone, where we used to go for our walk, and come to me there with Krassotkin in the evening ... and Perezvon ... I'll be waiting for you. Father, father!”
His voice broke. The three of them were silent, still embracing. Nina was crying quietly in her chair, and at last, seeing them all weep, “mamma” too burst into tears.
“Ilusha! Ilusha!” she cried.
Krassotkin suddenly freed himself from Ilusha's embrace.

“Good-bye, old man — mother's expecting me home for dinner,” he said quickly. “What a pity I didn't tell her! She'll be terribly anxious. But after dinner I'll come back to you for the whole day, for the whole evening, and I'll tell you all sorts of things, all sorts of things. And I'll bring Perezvon — but now I'll take him with me, because he'll start howling when I'm gone and bother you. Good-bye!”
And he ran out into the passage. He didn't want to cry, but in the passage he burst into tears. Alyosha found him crying.
“Kolya, you must be sure to keep your word and come, or he'll be terribly disappointed,” Alyosha said emphatically.
“I will! Oh, how I curse myself for not having come sooner!” muttered Kolya, crying, and no longer ashamed of it.
At that moment the captain flew out of the room and at once closed the door behind him. His face looked frenzied; his lips were trembling. He stood in front of the two and flung up his arms.

“I don't want a good boy! I don't want another boy!” he muttered in a wild whisper, clenching his teeth. “If I forget thee, Jerusalem, may my tongue —” He broke off with a sob and sank to his knees in front of the wooden bench. Pressing his fists against his head, he began sobbing with absurd whimpering cries, doing his utmost that his cries not be heard inside the room.
Kolya ran out into the street.
“Good-bye, Karamazov. Will you come yourself?” he cried sharply and angrily to Alyosha.
“I'll certainly come in the evening.”
“What was that he said about Jerusalem? What did he mean by that?”
“It's from the Bible. ‘If I forget thee, Jerusalem,' that is, if I forget what is most precious to me, if I let anything take its place, may —”
“I understand, that's enough! Mind you come. _Ici_, Perezvon!” he cried with positive ferocity to the dog, and with rapid strides he set off for home.
